title: AQA English Language Paper 1 Question 4: Evaluation (2026 Format)
description: How to answer AQA Paper 1 Question 4 from 2026: build a clear judgement, analyse methods, use precise evidence and develop a critical 20-mark evaluation.

children: Paper 1 Question 4 is the extended 20-mark reading task and assesses AO4: critical evaluation supported by textual references. From 2026, AQA removed the older framing in which a “student” made the statement. The task still gives you a viewpoint to evaluate, but the wording encourages a direct critical response supported by analysis of the writer’s methods.
Evaluation is not the same as analysis

Analysis asks how a choice works. Evaluation adds a judgement about how far an interpretation or statement is convincing. A strong response therefore needs an argument: you might largely agree, partly agree, qualify the statement, or show that the text creates a more complicated impression.
Build a line of argument first
Decide your overall position before writing: strongly agree, mostly agree, partly agree, or disagree.
Break the statement into key ideas. You do not have to treat every word as equally convincing.
Choose evidence from the specified section that lets you test the statement rather than merely illustrate it.
Analyse methods because they are evidence for your judgement, not because the question secretly becomes Question 2.
A four-part paragraph structure
Judgement: state a precise view about one part of the statement.
Evidence: select a short textual detail that genuinely tests that judgement.
Analysis: explain how the writer’s choice creates the impression.
Evaluation: return to the statement and explain why the evidence strengthens, weakens or complicates it.
Mini-example with invented material

Suppose a statement claims that a storm is presented as exciting rather than dangerous. An effective response might argue that the description initially creates exhilaration through rapid movement, but this is undercut when the narrative shifts to a trapped character. That contrast allows a more sophisticated judgement: the storm’s energy can be thrilling while its consequences remain threatening.
The phrase “to what extent” rewards control, not indecision. You can have a firm overall view while still recognising complexity.
What Level 4 thinking tends to do
Develops a convincing critical interpretation instead of repeating “I agree”.
Selects judicious details rather than using quotations because they are easy to spot.
Analyses the writer’s methods as part of the evaluation.
Considers impact and meaning in a way that is specific to the statement.
Builds connections between pieces of evidence so the argument develops.
Common mistakes
Starting every paragraph “I agree because…” without developing a real judgement.
Writing a language-analysis essay but barely referring back to the statement.
Using evidence from outside the specified lines.
Treating agreement as all-or-nothing when the text supports a nuanced interpretation.
Giving personal opinion with no textual analysis.
Practice drill
Take one evaluative statement about an unseen extract.
Write three possible judgements: agree, qualify, challenge.
Find one quotation that could support each judgement.
Choose the most convincing two or three and sequence them into an argument.
After each analytical sentence, add: “Therefore, this makes the statement…” and complete it precisely.
Final checklist
My response has an overall position.
Each paragraph tests the statement.
I used evidence only from the required section.
Methods are analysed in service of my judgement.
My final view is more developed than simply “I agree”.
